author: Carlos Martinez
title: Portland International Raceway iRacing guide: turn-in points and apexes
description: Learn Portland's fast technical sections, late-apex corners, and how track temperature swings affect grip through the day.

sections.p: Portland International Raceway is a 1.97-mile road course that demands precision over raw speed. The track has a reputation for punishing imprecision and rewarding smooth inputs. Most of the lap is broken into two very different halves: the flowing back section from Turn 1 through the Esses, and the tighter infield complex from Turn 7 onwards. Understanding how to carry speed through each section while staying within track limits will separate consistent drivers from those who fall off the pace or accumulate penalties.

Portland's elevation changes, camber variations, and weather sensitivity mean that what works on a cold morning will cost you tenths on a warm afternoon. The track is also famous for its outside curbing, which can either help you carry exit speed or dump you into the dirt if you misjudge the line. This guide covers the key technical sections, reference points that hold up across fuel loads and tire degradation, and how to adjust your approach when conditions shift.

sections.h2: The racing line through the back section: Turn 1 to the Esses

sections.p: Turn 1 is a moderate-speed right-hander that sets the tone for the lap. The entry is from the short main straight, and most drivers brake in a straight line before turning in. Turn-in happens roughly where the braking zone ends, around the 100-meter board. The apex is early in the corner, and the critical detail here is how early you pick up the throttle on exit. A smooth, progressive application of power onto the white exit curbing gives you a platform for the Esses.

The Esses (Turns 2 and 3) flow quickly once you establish rhythm. Turn 2 is a fast left-hander where most of your time is lost by braking too early or too hard. The key is trail braking to a late apex, allowing the car to settle as it unwinds. Many drivers brake as if they are entering Turn 2 in isolation and waste track on entry. Instead, think of Turns 1 and 2 as one flowing section: controlled exit from Turn 1 feeds into efficient trail braking into Turn 2. The apex of Turn 2 sits near the inside curb, and you need to clip it cleanly but not so hard that the car is unsettled for Turn 3.

Turn 3 is a tight right-hander immediately after Turn 2. The transition happens fast, and this is where car balance matters most. If the car is not settled from Turn 2, you will overdrive the entry to Turn 3 and either run wide or lock a wheel. The ideal line has minimal brake application between Turn 2 and Turn 3 because you should already be scrubbed down to the right speed. Turn-in to Turn 3 happens roughly where the curbing ends from Turn 2. The apex is inside, and the exit is where you want maximum track width to begin the run up to Turn 5.

list: Turn 1: Early brake, smooth exit throttle onto the white curb for momentum into the Esses
Turn 2: Trail brake to a late apex, do not brake as though this corner exists alone
Turn 3: Minimal brake input between Turns 2 and 3, clip the inside apex and use full exit width

sections.h2: Building momentum through the uphill and Turn 5

sections.p: Between Turn 3 and Turn 5 is a short uphill straight. Many drivers focus only on Turn 5 and miss the opportunity to build momentum here. The car naturally slows climbing the hill, so any small input errors or hesitation in throttle application will kill your exit speed. Commit to full throttle exiting Turn 3, stay on it through the hill, and do not lift until you need to for Turn 5.

Turn 5 is a fast left-hander that sits at the top of the hill. The entry is deceptive because the hill masks how fast you are going and the elevation makes the turn feel slower than it actually is. Brake in a straight line before the turn-in zone, which is roughly 50-60 meters before the apex. The apex is near the inside curb, and the corner is really about how much speed you carry through the middle. Use late apex principles here: sacrifice entry speed slightly to rotate the car and have full throttle on the exit. The outside curbing on exit is firm and will help you maintain line if you run it, but running too far out will hurt the following straights because you lose momentum.

sections.tip: Many drivers brake too hard into Turn 5 trying to make the corner feel easier to enter. Brake progressively and turn in late instead. This preserves exit speed and sets up the downhill run to Turn 7 much better than a defensive early apex.

sections.p: After Turn 5, the track descends downhill for several hundred meters. This is one of the few places where you can freely accelerate and gain speed without immediately having to manage a corner. Full throttle, smooth steering inputs, and trusting the car through the elevation change will keep you in control. Do not overdrive this section trying to make up time; the real gain is in clean execution at Turn 7.

Turn 7 is a right-hander that comes at you fast because of the downhill entry. The turn is faster than it initially appears, and many drivers unnecessarily brake hard or brake too early because the downhill momentum feels overwhelming. The brake point is at the 100-meter board or slightly before, depending on fuel and tire load. Turn-in happens after the brake zone ends, around the 50-meter board. The apex is early to middle, and the critical detail is not running out to the exit curb too early. Some cars will naturally push wide here, and fighting it by turning in too hard will only cause understeer and lock-up. Accept a slightly earlier apex and prioritize exit speed onto the short straight toward Turn 8.

Turns 8, 9, and 10 form a tight infield complex where precision and rhythm are everything. This section is where inconsistency costs the most time. A small error in Turn 8 will propagate through Turn 9 and ruin your Turn 10 exit.

Turn 8 is a left-hander with a short straight before it. You come off the main section accelerating and need to scrub speed quickly. Brake in a straight line, turn in relatively early to the turn, and aim for an early apex. This gives you a late exit on the curbing, which positions you perfectly for Turn 9. The temptation is to run a perfect geometric arc through Turn 8, but the track geometry actually rewards a tighter, earlier-apex approach.

Turn 9 is a quick right-hander immediately after Turn 8. The transition happens fast, and your exit from Turn 8 determines your entry to Turn 9. If you carried the throttle too long out of Turn 8, you will be overspeed for Turn 9 and will either lock a brake or run wide. If your exit is too slow, Turn 9 becomes a momentum-killer. The line through Turn 9 is relatively tight. Turn-in is direct, the apex is inside, and the exit should carry you to the right curbing for the run into Turn 10.

Turn 10 is the tightest corner on the circuit, a sharp right-hander that connects to the short back straight. This is a low-speed corner where you need smooth steering inputs and patience. Do not overload the tires on entry because you will lose front grip and understeer. Trail brake to a mid-to-late apex, and do not apply throttle aggressively until the car is fully rotated. The exit curb is minimal here, so most of your track width is on entry, not exit.

olist: Turn 8 left-hander: Brake hard, turn in early to early apex, carry throttle up and out to the outside curb for position into Turn 9
Turn 9 right-hander: Minimal brake into this quick transition, smooth steering and early mid-throttle application to load the tire
Turn 10 sharp right: Trail brake to mid apex, rotate the car fully, apply throttle smoothly once pointed toward the exit

sections.h2: Track limits, curbing, and how to read the day's conditions

sections.p: Portland's outside curbing is aggressive on several corners, particularly Turn 5 and Turn 7. Running the curbing cleanly is within the rules and will actually improve your lap time by maintaining trajectory and exit speed. However, the curbing can also unsettle the car if you hit it hard or at the wrong angle. Early in the session, use the curbing as a guide for where the track ends, not as a wall to bash through. As the session progresses and you trust the car, you can lean on the curbing for help maintaining line.

Track temperature swings at Portland affect grip significantly. A cold morning session and a warm afternoon session will feel like different tracks. On a cold day, the track will have less grip, and you will need to be smoother and more progressive on throttle application. Late-apex lines that work in warm conditions might feel loose early in the day. On a warm day, you can attack apexes more aggressively and carry higher entry speeds because there is more grip available. Pay attention to tire temperature as well. Cold tires will be slippery for the first lap or two, and braking points and turn-in zones will shift. As tires come in, you can move your turn-in points slightly later and brake slightly deeper.

Tire degradation over a longer stint also changes the reference points. As tires wear, they will feel less responsive, and you may need to be earlier on turn-in to maintain your line. The track will also rubber in as the session progresses, providing slightly more grip overall. Lean into the track's help when it shows up, rather than fighting against it with unnecessary inputs.

sections.tip: Run a consistent reference point between fuel loads by using trackside markers you can see from your cockpit: a billboard, signage, or a distinctive tree. This keeps your turn-in zone and brake points consistent even as fuel load, tire temperature, and track temperature shift throughout the day.

sections.h2: Putting it together: a sample lap

sections.p: A clean lap at Portland flows like this: aggressive trail braking into Turn 1 with a smooth exit onto the white curb. Flow through the Esses with minimal brake application between turns, clipping each apex and using the full track width. Build momentum uphill and carry it into the late-apex Turn 5. Commit to full throttle down the hill and manage the entry to Turn 7 without overdriving the brake. Execute the infield complex with precision, especially Turn 8 to Turn 9 transition. Finish strong out of Turn 10 onto the back straight and repeat. Each lap should feel similar, with small adjustments only for track temperature or tire condition. Consistency will beat raw pace at this circuit every time.

faqs.q: How early should I turn in at Turn 1?
faqs.a: Turn-in at Turn 1 happens roughly at or just past the 100-meter board. The key is to brake in a straight line, do not turn in too early or you will carry too much speed and run wide on exit. Smooth application of throttle after the apex gives you momentum into the Esses.

faqs.q: What's the biggest mistake through Turns 2 and 3?
faqs.a: Treating Turn 2 as an isolated corner by braking hard into it rather than trail braking, and then having to brake again before Turn 3. The Esses should flow as one section: scrub speed with light trail braking into Turn 2, apex it, and use that exit speed directly into Turn 3 with minimal additional brake input.

faqs.q: Why does Turn 5 feel so different at different times of day?
faqs.a: Turn 5 sits at the top of a hill, and the elevation combined with track temperature changes shifts how much grip is available. On a cold track, the tire is less responsive and you need a smoother, earlier approach. On a warm track or with warm tires, you can attack a later apex more aggressively. The elevation also masks your actual speed, making the turn feel slower than it is, so trust your braking point.

faqs.q: How do I maintain consistency through the infield complex across multiple laps?
faqs.a: Use visual reference points trackside rather than trying to count brake points: brake at a specific billboard or tree for Turn 8, turn in when you see a particular sign, apex where the curb is, and exit to the outer marking. Rhythm through Turns 8, 9, and 10 comes from repeating the same visual and physical inputs, not from trying to optimize each corner independently.
